maml:description.maml:para: Lists the certificates in the certificate stores of this computer, with when they expire and what is wrong with them.

Returns one object per certificate in the stores asked for, LocalMachine\My unless told otherwise: the store it is in, its subject, issuer and DNS names, its validity dates, how many whole days it has left, its signature algorithm and key, and the audit rules it breaks.
Two rules are checked:
- CRT-001: the certificate has expired, or expires within the warning window. The window is the value of ExpiringInDays, or 30 days without it. - CRT-002: it is signed with MD2, MD4, MD5 or SHA-1, or its key is too short: RSA under 2048 bits, EC under 256, or DSA of any size. The signature of a self-signed certificate, such as a root, is not checked: nobody verifies it, because a root is trusted for being in the store. Its key is checked like any other.
With ExpiringInDays, only the certificates that expire within that many days come out, the expired ones included. The certificates that expire first come first.
The stores are opened read-only, and only if they exist. If one store cannot be opened, the certificates of the others are still returned and an error says which store failed.
It only runs on Windows. Nothing is changed.

Lists only the certificates that expire within this many days, the expired ones included, and uses the same number of days as the warning window of rule CRT-001. A certificate with 13.9 days left counts as 13. Without this parameter every certificate is listed and the window is 30 days.
Whose stores to read: LocalMachine, the stores of the computer, or CurrentUser, the stores of the user running the command.

One or more stores to read. My is the Personal store, where most service certificates are; WebHosting is where IIS can keep its own; Remote Desktop holds the certificate of RDP; Root and CA hold the trusted roots and the intermediate authorities; TrustedPublisher, the publishers trusted to sign code.
This cmdlet takes no input from the pipeline.

One object per certificate, with the properties ComputerName, Store, Subject, Issuer, DnsNames, FriendlyName, Thumbprint, SerialNumber, NotBefore, NotAfter, DaysLeft, Status (Valid, Expiring, Expired or NotYetValid), SignatureAlgorithm, KeyAlgorithm (RSA, EC or DSA), KeySize, WeakReason, HasPrivateKey and Findings (the ids of the rules it breaks, separated by "; "). The default table shows Store, Subject, NotAfter, DaysLeft, Status and Findings.

maml:alert.maml:para: It does not check whether a certificate has been revoked, whether its chain is trusted on this computer, or whether its names match the service that uses it. To see what a server sends to its clients, including the intermediate certificates (rule CRT-003), use Get-WinOpsAuditTlsCertificate. These are audit rules CRT-001 and CRT-002.

maml:description.maml:para: Describes this computer: hardware, operating system, domain and installed updates.

Returns one object for the computer it runs on, read through CIM: who made it and which model it is, its serial number and firmware version, its processors and memory, its operating system, when it was installed and last started, the domain it belongs to, and how many updates are installed and when the last one was.
Every property is a plain value, so the object can be filtered, exported to CSV or JSON, or saved and compared with a later run. The list of updates itself comes from Get-WinOpsAuditUpdate.
If the updates cannot be read, the object is still returned with UpdateCount and LastUpdateInstalledOn empty, and an error says why: empty means unknown, not zero. If the computer, its firmware, its processors or its operating system cannot be read, the cmdlet stops with an error and returns nothing.
It only runs on Windows. Nothing is changed.
This cmdlet takes no input from the pipeline.

One object with the properties ComputerName, Domain, PartOfDomain, Manufacturer, Model, SerialNumber, BiosVersion, Processor, ProcessorCount, CoreCount, LogicalProcessorCount, MemoryGB, OperatingSystem, OSVersion, OSArchitecture, InstallDate, LastBootUpTime, UpdateCount and LastUpdateInstalledOn.

maml:alert.maml:para: The data comes from the CIM classes Win32_ComputerSystem, Win32_OperatingSystem, Win32_BIOS, Win32_Processor and Win32_QuickFixEngineering. MemoryGB is the memory Windows can use (TotalPhysicalMemory), a little less than what is installed. This is audit rule INV-001.

maml:description.maml:para: Lists the audit rules WinOpsAudit knows about.

Returns one object per audit rule: its id, the area it audits, what it looks for, how serious a finding is, and whether it is available yet or still planned. The objects can be filtered, sorted and exported like any other PowerShell output.
Nothing is audited and nothing is changed: this only reads the catalog that ships with the module.
Only the rules of these areas: Inventory, Certificates, FolderPermissions or ActiveDirectory.

One or more rule ids. Wildcards are allowed, for example `AD-*`. An exact id that matches no rule writes an error and the command goes on with the rest; a wildcard that matches nothing is not an error.
Rule ids, from the pipeline or from the Id property of the objects in it.
One object per rule, with the properties Id, Area, Title, Severity, Status and Session (the roadmap session that brings the rule).

maml:alert.maml:para: The catalog is in `Data/Rules.psd1` inside the module. A rule is Planned until its cmdlet, tests and help are written; then it is Available.

maml:description.maml:para: Lists the programs installed on this computer.

Returns one object per installed program: its name, version, publisher and install date, whether it is a 64-bit or a 32-bit program, and whether it is installed for the whole computer or only for the current user.
The programs are read from the uninstall keys of the registry, the same place "Installed apps" in Windows Settings reads them from: the 64-bit and 32-bit keys of the computer and the key of the current user. It never queries the CIM class Win32_Product, which makes Windows check, and sometimes repair, every MSI installation. Entries that "Installed apps" hides are left out too: parts of other programs (SystemComponent), updates of other programs, and entries with no name.
If one of the keys cannot be read, the programs of the others are still returned and an error says which key failed. An entry that cannot be opened is skipped with a warning that names it.
It only runs on Windows. Nothing is changed.

One or more program names. Wildcards are allowed, for example `*Java*`, and the case does not matter. An exact name that matches no installed program writes an error and the command goes on with the rest; a wildcard that matches nothing is not an error.
This cmdlet takes no input from the pipeline.

One object per program, with the properties ComputerName, Name, Version, Publisher, InstallDate, Architecture (x64, x86, or empty for programs of the current user, whose key does not say), Scope (Machine or CurrentUser) and UninstallKey (the name of its registry key). The default table shows Name, Version, Publisher, Architecture and Scope.

maml:alert.maml:para: Programs installed for other users who are not logged on are not listed: their part of the registry is only loaded while they are. Apps from the Microsoft Store are not listed either: they are not registered under the uninstall keys. It expects 64-bit Windows, as are Windows 11 and every Windows Server since 2008 R2: on 32-bit Windows each program would be listed twice. Why the registry and not Win32_Product is explained in ADR 0002 of the project. This is audit rule INV-002.

maml:description.maml:para: Connects to TLS servers and audits the certificate each one presents, and the chain it sends with it.

Opens a TLS connection to each server, reads the certificate it presents and the other certificates it sends, and closes the connection: nothing is sent after the handshake. Any certificate is accepted, because the point is to look at it, not to trust it.
Returns one object per server with the same description as Get-WinOpsAuditCertificate (subject, dates, days left, algorithm, key) and rules CRT-001 and CRT-002, plus what the server sends:
- CRT-003: the server does not send the intermediate certificates its chain needs. A client that has them from before (in its store, in its cache, or downloaded from the address written in the certificate) connects fine, and another one fails. So whether this computer can complete the chain proves nothing: the check builds the chain this computer would use, with everything it can find, and reports every intermediate in it that the server did not send. ChainStatus is Complete, MissingIntermediate, or UnknownIssuer when the chain does not reach a root this computer trusts; in that case it cannot tell who lacks the certificate, and no finding is reported.
Building the chain can download intermediate certificates from the addresses written in the certificates, as browsers do. Revocation is not checked.
A server that cannot be reached, or does not finish the handshake in time, writes an error that names it, and the command goes on with the others.
It runs on any system PowerShell 7 runs on. Nothing is changed.

Certificates of a private PKI, for servers whose chain this computer does not know. The self-signed ones are trusted as roots, instead of the roots of this computer; the others only help to build the chain. They are not treated as sent by the server: an intermediate found only here is still reported as missing.

One or more servers, by name or IP address. The name is also sent in the handshake (SNI), so a server with several sites presents the certificate of that name. Takes names from the pipeline, as text or as a property named ComputerName, HostName or DnsName.

Lists only the servers whose certificate expires within this many days, the expired ones included, and uses the same number of days as the warning window of rule CRT-001. Without this parameter every server is listed and the window is 30 days.
The TCP port, the same for every server. 443 unless told otherwise.
How long to wait for each server to accept the connection, and then for each step of the handshake, before giving up on it. 10 seconds unless told otherwise.
The names of the servers, as text or as a property named ComputerName, HostName or DnsName.

One object per server, with the properties ComputerName, Port, Protocol (the TLS version agreed), Subject, Issuer, DnsNames, Thumbprint, SerialNumber, NotBefore, NotAfter, DaysLeft, Status, SignatureAlgorithm, KeyAlgorithm, KeySize, WeakReason, SentCount (how many certificates the server sent besides its own), ChainStatus, MissingCertificate (the subjects of the certificates the server should have sent, or the unknown issuer) and Findings. The default table shows ComputerName, Port, Subject, DaysLeft, Status, ChainStatus and Findings.

maml:alert.maml:para: It does not check whether the names in the certificate match the server, whether the certificate has been revoked, or which TLS versions and ciphers the server accepts besides the one agreed. Why CRT-003 is judged from what the server sends, and not from whether this computer can build the chain, is explained in ADR 0003 of the project. These are audit rules CRT-001, CRT-002 and CRT-003.

command:example.maml:title: --------- Example 4: Servers of a private PKI ---------

maml:introduction.maml:para: ```powershell $pki = Get-ChildItem -Path Cert:\LocalMachine\Root, Cert:\LocalMachine\CA | Where-Object Subject -like '*O=Contoso*' Import-Csv .\servers.csv | Get-WinOpsAuditTlsCertificate -CertificateAuthority $pki | Where-Object ChainStatus -ne 'Complete' ```
The CSV file needs a column named ComputerName (or HostName). The certificates of the private PKI let the check build the chain even on a computer that does not trust that PKI.

maml:description.maml:para: Lists the updates installed on this computer.

Returns one object per installed update, read from the CIM class Win32_QuickFixEngineering: its KB number, its kind (Update, Security Update...), when it was installed and by whom. The oldest come first; updates with no known date come before them.
Windows keeps the install date as text, in more than one format. It is turned into a date, and left empty when Windows does not record it, rather than guessed.
It only runs on Windows. Nothing is changed.
This cmdlet takes no input from the pipeline.
One object per update, with the properties ComputerName, HotFixId, Description, InstalledOn and InstalledBy. The default table leaves out ComputerName and shows the date without the time.

maml:alert.maml:para: Win32_QuickFixEngineering lists the updates of Windows itself installed through Windows Update or as packages. It does not list updates of other products (Office, for example) or of Microsoft Defender's definitions. Get-HotFix reads the same class; the tests check on Windows that both give the same updates and dates. This is part of audit rule INV-001.
